article_lead.description: a display of numerical data in adjacent intervals whose bar areas reveal how the observations are distributed across the measurement scale

new_bank_questions.title: A density bar taller than one
new_bank_questions.body: Ten observations fall in two adjacent bins. Six are in $[0,0.2)$ and four are in $[0.2,1)$. Find the heights and areas of a density histogram. Is a bar height greater than one an error?
new_bank_questions.answer: The widths are $0.2$ and $0.8$. The density heights are $6/(10\cdot0.2)=3$ and $4/(10\cdot0.8)=0.5$. The areas are $3\cdot0.2=0.6$ and $0.5\cdot0.8=0.4$, summing to one. Height $3$ is valid: density is probability per unit of the horizontal scale, while each bar's area is its probability share.

new_bank_questions.title: Shifting histogram boundaries
new_bank_questions.body: The measurements are $0.4,0.6,1.4,1.6,2.4$. Count them first in $[0,1),[1,2),[2,3)$, then in $[-0.5,0.5),[0.5,1.5),[1.5,2.5)$. What changes, and what should that tell you about interpreting a peak from five values?
new_bank_questions.answer: The first grid has counts $(2,2,1)$. The shifted grid has counts $(1,2,2)$. The data have not changed: one measurement moves from the first bar to the second, and another from the second to the third because the boundaries moved. A peak or asymmetry inferred from five binned observations is sensitive to that choice; inspect the raw values and several reasonable grids.
